messages.author: f9dee1336056abf1
messages.subject: not passing gof tests
parts:
Hi all,

My work is currently looking at comparing bird density estimates obtained from point count and line transect surveys (carried out in the same location, at very similar times, etc.). It is a multi-species dataset, so the code creates a table for each species of all observations, and adds new rows for the sample labels at which the species was not observed.

One group of species which is of particular interest is ground flushers (i.e. quails, etc.) as one could expect point count methodology does not lend itself to seeing them, whereas line transects do. However, in order to get a sufficient number of observations for this group from point counts, I have had to amalgamate 4 species together.

When running the code to estimate densities, all works fine for point counts, but it does not pass goodness of fit tests for line transects. I have attached a photo showing the half-normal function fitted to the line transect data. It is frustrating as, to my untrained eye, it doesn't look particularly bad. Could it be because detection probability is greater than 1 at the start?

Thanks in advance,


Oscar

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] not passing gof tests
parts:
Hello Oscar

Line transect data that have a spike close to the line are notoriously difficult to model.  You face the unenviable decision between using a flexible model that will fit the spike and produce very large estimates of abundance, or use a less flexible model that does not provide good fit to the data.  The question boils down to whether it is plausible the detectability changes as radically between histogram bars 1 and 2 as the histogram depicts.

messages.author: f9dee1336056abf1
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] not passing gof tests
parts:
Hi Eric,

I suspect the detectability really would change that much; often ground flusher species will be flushed from the transect line, as unless observers are very close to them they will simply sit tight, or skulk away through long grasses, remaining unobserved. Because of that I would imagine that detectability would fall away significantly pretty quickly as you move away from the transect line.

Oscar

messages.author: 7482eee8d2863d12
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] not passing gof tests
parts:
Hi Oscar and Eric,

I'm not sure what the scale was on the x-axis but I'm guessing km, so
your first bin is 10m. If it's reasonable to assume that all birds
within 10m flush, then you might get a more reliable estimate by
treating this survey as a strip transect, and truncating at 10m. The
alternative is to try to model this very difficult detection function.

I wonder if you can alter the field methods to try to get birds farther
out to flush -- e.g., by taking a trained dog with you, or two observers
walking a short distance apart, side by side (it's important to be sure
where the line is in this case, to obtain accurate distance measurements).

Best wishes, Len
